text: A volcano erased summer, and ended up inventing the bicycle.
April eighteen fifteen.
Tambora goes off, the biggest eruption in recorded history.
A hundred and fifty cubic kilometres of rock, forty kilometres into the sky.
It killed more than seventy thousand people, mostly of hunger, and it changed the weather of the whole planet.
Eighteen sixteen came, the year without a summer.
It snowed in June.
Harvests failed from Ireland to China.
They called it eighteen hundred and froze to death.
Oat prices rose eight times.
On Lake Geneva, rained in at the Villa Diodati, an eighteen-year-old named Mary Shelley got so bored she wrote Frankenstein.
In Baden, a forester and baron named Karl Drais had the same problem.
The oats were gone, and with them, the horses.
So he built a better horse. Two wheels, a beam, a saddle.
No pedals.
The Laufmaschine.
You push off the ground with your feet.
On June the twelfth, eighteen seventeen, he rode from Mannheim to Schwetzingen, fourteen kilometres in under an hour, on wood, with zero horses.
Luckily, it worked.
Unluckily, the riders didn't.
Mannheim banned them from the pavements.
Milan, London and New York followed.
Because a volcano is a chimney that burps a parasol into space.
Dim the sun, and the wheat gives up, the oats give up, the horse gives up, the road is yours.
Pedals came in the eighteen sixties, then chains, then gears. A volcano's bad mood became the most-ridden vehicle on Earth.
So next time someone flies past on a bicycle, that's Mount Tambora's fault.
One eruption.
One lost summer.
One man, no horse.
